title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: How Agriculture Was Held Back in Early Europe, After the Fall of the Roman Empire

When the German and Scythian peoples overran the western provinces of the Roman empire, the chaos that followed such an enormous upheaval went on for several centuries. The barbarians plundered and brutalised the old inhabitants, and this cut off trade between the towns and the countryside. The towns emptied, the land was left untilled, and the western provinces of Europe, which had been fairly wealthy under Roman rule, sank into the deepest poverty and barbarism. While this disorder lasted, the chiefs and leading men of these nations seized, or simply grabbed, most of the land in these countries. Much of it lay uncultivated, but no part of it, cultivated or not, was without an owner. It was all monopolised, and most of it by a handful of great landowners.

This early monopolising of uncultivated land was a serious problem, but it might have been only a temporary one. The estates could soon have been split up again into small lots, either through inheritance or through sale. But the law of primogeniture stopped them from being divided by inheritance, and the introduction of entails stopped them from being broken into small lots by sale.

When land is treated merely as a means of subsistence and enjoyment, just like movable property, the natural rule of inheritance divides it, as it does movables, among all the children of the family, since a father may be assumed to care equally about the livelihood and comfort of every one of them. This natural rule of inheritance is exactly what the Romans followed: they drew no more distinction between elder and younger, or between male and female, in passing on land than we do in handing out movable goods. But once land was seen as a means not just of subsistence but of power and protection, people thought it better for it to pass undivided to a single heir. In those lawless times, every great landlord was a kind of petty prince. His tenants were his subjects. He acted as their judge, in some ways as their lawmaker in peacetime, and as their commander in war. He waged war as he saw fit, often against his neighbours and sometimes against his own king. So the security of a landed estate, and the protection its owner could give to the people living on it, depended on how large it was. To divide the estate was to wreck it, leaving every piece of it open to being crushed and absorbed by raids from its neighbours. The law of primogeniture therefore came to govern the inheritance of landed estates, not right away but over time, for the same reason it has generally governed the succession of monarchies, though not always from their very beginning. So that division does not weaken the power, and therefore the security, of the monarchy, the crown must pass whole to one of the children. Which child should receive so important a preference has to be settled by some general rule, one based not on the uncertain matter of personal merit but on some plain, obvious difference that cannot be argued about. Among the children of one family the only undeniable differences are sex and age. Males are universally preferred to females, and when everything else is equal, the elder everywhere takes precedence over the younger. This is the origin of the right of primogeniture and of what we call lineal succession.

Laws often stay in force long after the circumstances that first prompted them, and that alone made them reasonable, have disappeared. In Europe today, the owner of a single acre of land is just as secure in his possession as the owner of a hundred thousand acres. Yet the right of primogeniture is still respected, and because it is, of all institutions, the one best suited to feed the pride of family rank, it is likely to last for many more centuries. In every other respect, nothing could be more at odds with the true interest of a large family than a rule that enriches one child by leaving all the others destitute.

Entails are the natural offspring of the law of primogeniture. They were introduced to preserve a fixed line of inheritance, the very idea of which primogeniture had first suggested, and to stop any part of the original estate from being taken out of the intended line by gift, bequest, or sale, whether through the foolishness or the bad luck of any of its successive owners. The Romans knew nothing of them. Neither their substitutions nor their fideicommissa bear any resemblance to entails, although some French lawyers have chosen to dress up the modern device in the language and trappings of those ancient ones.

When great landed estates were a kind of principality, entails may not have been unreasonable. Like the so-called fundamental laws of certain monarchies, they could often keep the security of thousands from being put at risk by the whim or recklessness of one man. But in Europe today, where small estates as well as great ones draw their security from the laws of their country, nothing could be more utterly absurd. Entails rest on the most absurd of all assumptions: that each successive generation does not have an equal right to the earth and everything it holds, but that the property of the present generation should be tied down and controlled according to the wishes of people who died, perhaps, five hundred years ago. Even so, entails are still respected through most of Europe, especially in those countries where noble birth is a required qualification for holding civil or military honours. They are thought necessary to keep up the nobility's exclusive claim to the great offices and honours of their country. Having seized one unjust advantage over the rest of their fellow citizens, the nobility are then granted another, so that poverty does not make the first one look ridiculous. The common law of England is said to detest perpetuities, and they are accordingly more restricted there than in any other European monarchy, though even England is not entirely free of them. In Scotland, more than a fifth, perhaps more than a third, of all the land in the country is currently believed to be under strict entail.

In this way, great stretches of uncultivated land were not only monopolised by particular families but locked up so that they could not, as far as possible, ever be divided again. Yet it rarely happens that a great landowner is a great improver of land. In the lawless times that produced these barbarous institutions, the great proprietor was busy enough defending his own territory or extending his power and authority over his neighbours' land. He had no time to spare for cultivating and improving the soil. When law and order were established and gave him that time, he often lacked the desire, and almost always lacked the necessary skills. If the cost of running his household and supporting himself matched or outran his income, as it very often did, he had no capital left to invest in improvement. If he was thrifty, he generally found it more profitable to spend his yearly savings on buying new land than on improving the estate he already had. Improving land profitably, like any other commercial venture, demands close attention to small savings and small gains, and a man born to a great fortune, however naturally frugal, is very rarely capable of that. His situation naturally inclines him to care more about ornament, which pleases his fancy, than about profit, which he has so little need of. The fine cut of his clothes, his carriage, his house, and his furniture are things he has been taught to worry over since childhood. The cast of mind this habit produces stays with him when he turns to improving land. He may beautify four or five hundred acres near his house at ten times what the land is worth even after all his improvements, and he finds that if he were to improve his whole estate in the same way, and he has little appetite for any other, he would be bankrupt before he had finished a tenth of it. In both parts of the United Kingdom there are still some great estates that have passed without a break through the same family since the time of feudal anarchy. Compare the present state of those estates with the holdings of the small proprietors nearby, and you will need no other proof of how badly such vast property serves improvement.

If little improvement could be expected from such great proprietors, even less could be hoped for from the people who worked the land under them. In early Europe, those who occupied the land were all tenants at will. They were all, or nearly all, slaves, though their slavery was milder than the kind known among the ancient Greeks and Romans, or even in our West Indian colonies. They were regarded as belonging more directly to the land than to their master. They could therefore be sold along with the land, but not separately. They could marry, provided the master agreed, and he could not afterwards break up the marriage by selling husband and wife to different buyers. If he maimed or killed any of them, he faced some penalty, though usually a small one. They could not, however, own property. Whatever they acquired belonged to their master, who could take it from them whenever he pleased. Any cultivation and improvement carried out by such slaves was really carried out by their master. He bore the cost. The seed, the livestock, and the farming tools were all his. The benefit was his. Such slaves could gain nothing but their daily upkeep. So in this case it was really the proprietor himself who occupied his own land and cultivated it through his own bondmen. This kind of slavery still survives in Russia, Poland, Hungary, Bohemia, Moravia, and other parts of Germany. Only in the western and south-western provinces of Europe has it gradually been abolished completely.

But if great improvements are rarely to be expected from great proprietors, they are least of all to be expected when those proprietors use slaves as their workers. The experience of every age and nation, I believe, shows that work done by slaves, though it seems to cost only their upkeep, turns out in the end to be the most expensive of all. A man who can own no property has no interest except to eat as much and work as little as he can. Any work he does beyond what is needed to pay for his own upkeep can only be wrung out of him by force, never by any motive of his own. Both Pliny and Columella note how much corn-growing declined in ancient Italy, and how unprofitable it became to the master, once it fell into the hands of slaves. In Aristotle's day, things had been no better in ancient Greece. Discussing the ideal republic described in Plato's Laws, Aristotle says that to support five thousand idle men, the number of warriors thought necessary for its defence, along with their women and servants, would require a territory of limitless size and fertility, like the plains of Babylon.

Man's pride makes him love to dominate, and nothing galls him more than having to stoop to persuading his inferiors. So wherever the law allows it and the nature of the work permits it, he will generally prefer the labour of slaves to that of free men. Growing sugar and tobacco can bear the cost of slave cultivation. Growing corn, it seems, in the present age cannot. In the English colonies, whose main product is corn, by far the greater part of the work is done by free men. The Quakers of Pennsylvania recently resolved to free all their negro slaves, and the fact that they could agree to this suggests their slaves cannot have been very numerous. Had the slaves made up any large share of their property, no such resolution could ever have been passed. In our sugar colonies, by contrast, all the work is done by slaves, and in our tobacco colonies a very large part of it. The profits of a sugar plantation in any of our West Indian colonies are generally far greater than those of any other kind of cultivation known in Europe or America, and the profits of a tobacco plantation, though lower than those of sugar, are higher than those of corn, as has already been pointed out. Both crops can bear the cost of slave cultivation, but sugar can bear it even better than tobacco. Accordingly, the number of negroes is much larger, in proportion to whites, in our sugar colonies than in our tobacco colonies.

The slave cultivators of ancient times were gradually replaced by a kind of farmer known today in France as metayers. In Latin they are called Coloni Partiarii. They have been out of use in England for so long that I know of no English name for them. The proprietor supplied them with the seed, livestock, and farming tools, in short the whole capital needed to work the farm. The produce was split evenly between the proprietor and the farmer, after setting aside whatever was judged necessary to maintain the capital, which was returned to the proprietor whenever the farmer left or was turned out of the farm.

Land held by such tenants is really cultivated at the proprietor's expense, just as much as land worked by slaves. There is, however, one crucial difference between them. These tenants, being free men, can acquire property, and since they receive a fixed share of the land's produce, they have an obvious interest in making the whole produce as large as possible, so that their own share will be large too. A slave, by contrast, who can gain nothing but his upkeep, looks after his own comfort by making the land yield as little as possible beyond that upkeep. It was probably partly because of this advantage, and partly because of the encroachments that the sovereigns, always wary of the great lords, gradually encouraged their serfs to make against the lords' authority, encroachments that seem at least to have made this kind of servitude thoroughly inconvenient, that villeinage gradually died out across most of Europe. The exact time and manner in which so important a change came about is one of the most obscure points in modern history. The Church of Rome claims great credit for it, and it is certain that as early as the twelfth century, Alexander III issued a bull for the general emancipation of slaves. This, however, seems to have been more a pious exhortation than a law demanding strict obedience from the faithful. Slavery went on almost everywhere for several centuries afterwards, until it was gradually abolished by the combined working of the two interests just mentioned, that of the proprietor on one side and that of the sovereign on the other. A serf, once freed and at the same time allowed to keep possession of the land, having no capital of his own, could work it only with what the landlord advanced to him, and so must have been what the French call a metayer.

Yet it could never be in the interest even of this last kind of cultivator to put any part of the small savings he might set aside from his own share of the produce into further improving the land, because the landlord, who put in nothing, was to receive half of whatever it produced. The tithe, which is only a tenth of the produce, is found to be a very great obstacle to improvement. A charge amounting to one half, then, must have been an effective barrier to it. A metayer might have an interest in making the land yield as much as the proprietor's capital could draw out of it, but he could never have an interest in mixing any of his own capital into it. In France, where five-sixths of the whole kingdom is said to be still occupied by this kind of cultivator, the proprietors complain that their metayers seize every chance to use their master's cattle for carting rather than farming, because in carting they keep all the profit themselves, whereas in farming they share it with the landlord. This kind of tenant still exists in some parts of Scotland, where they are called steelbow tenants. The old English tenants whom Chief-Baron Gilbert and Dr Blackstone describe as having been bailiffs of the landlord rather than farmers in the proper sense were probably of the same kind.

This kind of tenantry was succeeded, though very slowly, by farmers in the proper sense, who worked the land with their own capital and paid the landlord a fixed rent. When such farmers hold a lease for a set number of years, they may sometimes find it worth their while to invest part of their capital in further improving the farm, because they may sometimes expect to recover it, with a good profit, before the lease runs out. Even so, the position of these farmers was for a long time extremely insecure, and still is in many parts of Europe. Before their term was up, they could be legally evicted from their leases by a new buyer, and in England even by the fictitious legal device of a common recovery. If they were thrown out illegally by their master's violence, the legal action by which they sought redress was very inadequate. It did not always restore them to possession of the land but gave them damages that never matched their real loss. Even in England, perhaps the country in Europe where the yeomanry has always been most respected, it was not until about the fourteenth year of Henry VII that the action of ejectment was devised, by which the tenant recovers not just damages but possession, and in which his claim is not necessarily settled by the unpredictable verdict of a single assize. This action has proved so effective a remedy that in modern practice, when a landlord needs to sue for possession of the land, he rarely uses the actions that properly belong to him as landlord, the writ of right or the writ of entry, but instead sues in the name of his tenant by the writ of ejectment. In England, therefore, the tenant's security is equal to the proprietor's. In England, besides, a lease for life worth forty shillings a year counts as a freehold and entitles the holder to a vote for a member of parliament; and since a large part of the yeomanry hold freeholds of this kind, the whole class becomes worthy of respect from their landlords because of the political weight it gives them. There is, I believe, nowhere in Europe except England any case of a tenant building on land for which he had no lease, trusting that his landlord's honour would not take advantage of so important an improvement. These laws and customs, so favourable to the yeomanry, have perhaps done more for the present greatness of England than all their much-praised commercial regulations put together.

The law that secures the longest leases against successors of every kind is, as far as I know, unique to Great Britain. It was introduced into Scotland as early as 1449, by a law of James II. Its benefits, however, have been much hampered by entails, since heirs of entail are generally barred from granting leases for any long term of years, often for more than a single year. A recent act of parliament has somewhat loosened these restrictions, though they are still far too tight. In Scotland, besides, since no leasehold gives a vote for a member of parliament, the yeomanry are for this reason less respected by their landlords than in England.

In other parts of Europe, once it was found convenient to protect tenants against both heirs and buyers, the length of that protection was still kept very short, in France, for example, to nine years from the start of the lease. In that country it has indeed lately been extended to twenty-seven years, still too short a period to encourage the tenant to make the most important improvements. The landowners were once the lawmakers of every part of Europe, so the laws about land were all designed to serve what they took to be the proprietor's interest. They had imagined it was in his interest that no lease granted by any of his predecessors should stop him from enjoying the full value of his land over a long span of years. Greed and injustice are always short-sighted, and they failed to foresee how much this rule would hold back improvement, and so, in the long run, hurt the landlord's own real interest.

The farmers, too, besides paying rent, were once supposed to be bound to perform a great many services for the landlord, services that were rarely either spelled out in the lease or fixed by any precise rule, but were set by the custom and usage of the manor or barony. Being almost entirely arbitrary, these services exposed the tenant to many forms of harassment. In Scotland, the abolition of all services not precisely specified in the lease has, within a few years, greatly improved the condition of the country's yeomanry.

The public services the yeomanry owed were no less arbitrary than the private ones. Building and maintaining the highways, a duty that still exists, I believe, everywhere, though with different degrees of harshness in different countries, was not the only one. Whenever the king's troops, his household, or his officers of any kind passed through any part of the country, the yeomanry were bound to supply them with horses, carriages, and provisions at a price set by the purveyor. Great Britain is, I believe, the only monarchy in Europe where the burden of purveyance has been entirely abolished. It still exists in France and Germany.

The public taxes they were subject to were as irregular and oppressive as the services. The old lords, though extremely reluctant to grant their sovereign any money themselves, readily let him tax their tenants, which they called tallaging them, and lacked the foresight to see how much this would in the end affect their own income. The taille, as it still exists in France, can serve as an example of those old tallages. It is a tax on the supposed profits of the farmer, which they reckon from the amount of capital he keeps on the farm. So it is in his interest to appear to have as little as possible, and therefore to invest as little as possible in cultivating the land and nothing at all in improving it. Should any capital happen to build up in a French farmer's hands, the taille amounts almost to a ban on its ever being put into the land. This tax, besides, is thought to dishonour anyone who pays it and to drag him down below not only the rank of a gentleman but even that of a burgher, and anyone who rents another's land becomes liable to it. No gentleman, nor even any burgher who has capital, will accept such a humiliation. So this tax not only stops the capital that accumulates on the land from being used to improve it but also drives all other capital away. The old tenths and fifteenths, so common in England in former times, seem, as far as they touched the land, to have been taxes of the same kind as the taille.

Under all these discouragements, little improvement could be expected from those who occupied the land. That class of people, even with all the freedom and security the law can give, must always improve under great handicaps. The farmer, compared with the proprietor, is like a merchant who trades with borrowed money compared with one who trades with his own. The capital of both may grow, but with only equal good management the borrower's must always grow more slowly, because so large a share of the profits is eaten up by the interest on the loan. In the same way, land worked by a farmer must, with only equal good management, be improved more slowly than land worked by the proprietor, because so large a share of the produce is eaten up by the rent, which, had the farmer been the proprietor, he might have put into further improving the land. The farmer's position, besides, is by its very nature lower than the proprietor's. Through most of Europe, the yeomanry are regarded as a lower class of people, beneath even the better sort of tradesmen and mechanics, and throughout Europe beneath the great merchants and master manufacturers. So it can seldom happen that a man with any considerable capital would leave the higher station to put himself in a lower one. Even in Europe's present condition, then, little capital is likely to move from any other occupation into improving land by way of farming. More does so, perhaps, in Great Britain than in any other country, though even there the great fortunes employed in farming in some places have generally been built up by farming, which is, of all trades, perhaps the one in which capital is usually built up most slowly. After the small proprietors, however, rich and great farmers are in every country the chief improvers of land. There are perhaps more of them in England than in any other European monarchy. In the republican governments of Holland and of Berne in Switzerland, the farmers are said to be no worse than those of England.

On top of all this, the old policy of Europe was unfavourable to the improvement and cultivation of land, whether carried on by the proprietor or by the farmer. First, there was the general ban on exporting corn without a special licence, which seems to have been an almost universal rule. Second, there were the restraints placed on the inland trade, not only in corn but in nearly every other product of the farm, through the absurd laws against engrossers, regraters, and forestallers, and through the privileges of fairs and markets. It has already been shown how the ban on exporting corn, combined with some encouragement given to importing foreign corn, held back the cultivation of ancient Italy, naturally the most fertile country in Europe and at that time the seat of the world's greatest empire. How far such restraints on the inland trade in corn, joined to the general ban on its export, must have discouraged the cultivation of countries less fertile and less favourably placed, is perhaps not very easy to imagine.
